This vignette explains *why* aidR is built the way it is. For a hands-on walkthrough, see `vignette("aidR")`; for platform-specific details, see the `format-*` vignettes.

## Goal: one interface, many platforms

Every AID platform exports the same underlying concepts (CGM readings, basal delivery, boluses, carbohydrate intake) but encodes them completely differently: different file layouts, column names, units, languages, and levels of detail. aidR's central design goal is that downstream analysis code should not need to know which platform a participant's data came from. Everything upstream of `parse_data(clean_files = TRUE)` is platform-specific; everything downstream works on a small, fixed set of standardized data frames.

## Detecting formats from content, not filenames

`parse_data()` never looks at a file's name or extension (beyond filtering out obviously irrelevant extensions like `.png`/`.pdf`/`.txt`) to decide which platform it came from. Instead, each platform has an `.is_<platform>_format.aidR()` function that inspects the file's actual structure:

- exact header match, for platforms with stable, English, machine-generated headers (YourLoops, Tandem Source);
- structural fingerprints, for platforms whose headers vary by account language (Glooko: first-line pattern + column count/type; mylife: number of dot-separated header fields);
- content markers, for single-file, multi-section platforms (CareLink: `-------` section separators; Tidepool: presence of a `"CGM"` sheet in the workbook).

This is why users can drop a folder containing exports from several participants and several platforms (even nested inside `.zip` archives) into `parse_data()` and have every file routed to the right parser automatically -- see `vignette("aidR")` for an example.

## A common S3 interface per platform

Each platform implements the same two-function contract:

- `read_<platform>(id, filename)` reads one file and returns an object of class `<platform>`, wrapping the raw, unstandardized content.
- `clean.<platform>(data, id, ...)`, an S3 method for the generic `clean()`, turns that raw object into a named list of data frames.

`.process_file.aidR()` is the only place that knows about all platforms: it tries each `.is_<platform>_format.aidR()` in turn, calls the matching `read_<platform>()`, and (if `clean_files = TRUE`) dispatches to `clean()`. Adding a new platform means adding a new `read_*`/`clean.*`/`.is_*_format.aidR()` triplet and one new branch in that dispatch function -- nothing else in the package needs to change.

## Standardizing the core types, preserving the rest

Regardless of platform, `clean.<platform>()` always tries to produce some subset of five standardized data frames:

- **`cgm`**: `timestamp`, `value` (mg/dL)
- **`basal`**: `timestamp`, `duration`, `rate`
- **`bolus`**: `timestamp`, `type`, `total`, `normal`, `extended`
- **`carbs`**: `timestamp`, `carbs`, `label`, `estimated_absorption_duration`
- **`SMBG`**: `timestamp`, `value` (mg/dL)

Every standardized data frame also carries `id`, `format` (the source platform) and `timezone_offset` (in hours; `NA` where a platform only reports local time), so that data from different platforms can be safely combined -- see `vignette("aidR")`, "Merging data across participants".

Not every platform reports every core type (mylife, for example, only ever reports `bolus` and `carbs`), and platforms routinely report additional information that has no equivalent elsewhere (CareLink's sensor calibrations and device-change events; Tidepool's pump-setting sheets; Glooko's exercise and medication logs). Rather than force-fitting these into the standardized schema or silently dropping them, `clean.<platform>()` preserves them under their own, platform-specific name. The five core types are the contract every platform is normalized to; everything else is kept, unopinionated, for platform-specific analyses.

## Merging: per file, then per participant, then across participants

Merging happens in three, increasingly coarse-grained stages:

1. **Per file**: `read_<platform>()`/`clean.<platform>()` process one file at a time (a single CSV or `.xlsx`; for multi-sheet/multi-section platforms like Tidepool and CareLink, one call already produces several data types).
2. **Per participant**: `.merge_per_id.aidR()` (called internally at the end of `parse_data()`) row-binds all files belonging to one participant, by data type -- regardless of how many files or platforms they came from -- sorts each resulting data frame by `timestamp`, harmonizes column types that disagree across files (e.g. one file reporting a column as logical because it happened to be all-`NA`, another as character), and drops exact duplicate rows.
3. **Across participants**: `merge_all()` row-binds the per-participant lists into one long-format data frame per data type, adding the `id` column needed to tell participants apart.

Keeping these stages separate means a single participant's data (`parse_data()`'s return value) is always a complete, directly usable object on its own -- useful for per-participant checks and plots -- while `merge_all()` remains a thin, purely mechanical last step for population-level analysis.

## Cleaning, filtering and checking are separate steps

`parse_data(clean_files = TRUE)` only standardizes column layout and units -- it does not remove implausible values or check for completeness. Those are deliberately separate, opt-in steps:

- `filter_CGM()` truncates implausible CGM values and downsamples duplicate/overlapping readings to a regular time interval. It is applied *after* parsing, so `parse_data(clean_files = FALSE)` still gives access to completely raw values for debugging.
- `check_completeness()`/`check_completeness_range()` only warn about missing data types or missing days; they never modify data. This keeps "is my data as expected" checks independent of any filtering decisions.

## Conversion functions are one-way, best-effort exports

`get_iglu_format()` and `write_DIAX_format()` (see `vignette("aidR")`, "Converting to other formats") both consume the *standardized* data frames, never platform-specific raw data. This means they work identically regardless of which platform a participant's data came from, at the cost of only being able to export what the standardized schema captures (e.g. `write_DIAX_format()` cannot include CareLink's sensor-calibration events, since DIAX has no field for them).
